store.0: I am a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite packed with higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to. It's surreal to think about how far I've come since my freshman year, when I was learning about simple data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even basic quantum computing. It's exciting to see how much I've grown as a student.
store.1: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a huge fan of theory when it connects directly to real-world problem-solving, like optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The kind of problems that fascinate me are those that require dynamic programming approaches or approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It can be mind-bending at times, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great; she has a knack for explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll put up a problem on the board that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time, and then she'll show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing.
store.2: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second hardest. It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is definitely an adventure. We have to collaborate with people who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas of what the final product should look like. But that's also the beauty of it, right? In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle everything from concurrency issues to node failures gracefully. It's nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a single misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.
store.3: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take. My professor is actually from the industry; he worked on a couple of indie games that got some traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even some user experience design. It's incredibly fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, and it was all about finding the perfect balance for the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.
store.4: I also have an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I initially thought might be intimidating, but I'm actually enjoying it now. The professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than just math. Of course, there is math involved, like linear algebra, but it's balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not building actual quantum computers, but we're modeling algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff that's changing how I approach problems.
store.5: I'm also taking a Capstone Project course, which is basically the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group and I decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It sounds fancy, but essentially, we're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts by analyzing a firehose of tweets or posts for words that suggest a disaster or crisis. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major: database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to stay organized. One person on our team is the designated Scrum Master, so we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.
store.6: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it applies to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. It's great to sit back and analyze abstract ideas sometimes. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was fascinating. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.
store.7: I'm juggling a typical college schedule. Mondays and Wednesdays are packed. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload.
store.8: The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. Capstone alone can consume around ten hours a week, more if we encounter a major bug or if the model isn't training properly. The Distributed Systems project is another time-sucking endeavor. My group meets at least twice a week, and we rely on Slack or Discord to stay updated. Coordinating five different people's schedules can be a logistical nightmare. However, despite the stress, it's also exhilarating. This is one of my last chances to fully immerse myself in an academic project without the pressures of a real-world job environment. It's a great opportunity to learn and grow.
store.9: I'm having a blast overall. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but at this stage, I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, especially if something's due the next day and I'm stuck debugging. However, it's no longer as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a great feeling.
